When Geralt refused to lower his sword, Stregobor realized that he must've been similarly influenced and directed the attention of the villagers who had come to see what had happened to the men Geralt had killed. This caused the townspeople, Marilka included, to revolt against Geralt. They threw stones at him, as Renfri predicted they would, until he was forced to leave her body behind. As they parted, Stregobor confronted Geralt with the fact that he had made a choice and taken a side in the dispute between him and Renfri after all, and he suspected it would haunt Geralt.[1]

For the massacre he committed, he earned the infamous nickname "The Butcher of Blaviken" due to the aftermath of his fight with Renfri and her men, and the villagers mistakenly believed him to be a ruthless killer. For this reason, Geralt kept Renfri's brooch as a reminder never to interfere in human disputes again. 

### An Encounter with Elves[]

### An Encounter with Elves[]

Nine years after the events of Blaviken, Geralt was approached while drinking at a tavern in Posada by a bard named Jaskier, who insisted that Geralt review the poorly received musical performance he had just given. Geralt told Jaskier that the creatures in his song don't exist, and Jaskier realized that he was a witcher, which he announced to the bar. A tavern patron named Nettly overheard and offered to pay Geralt 100 ducats if he killed a "devil" that had been stealing the hamlet's grain. Geralt agreed to the job, but only for 150 ducats. Jaskier—to Geralt's chagrin—decided to tag along during Geralt's search for the creature. During that time, he offered his services spreading around the stories of "The Butcher of Blaviken," to which Geralt responded by hitting him in the gut. Understanding that Geralt resented being known that way, he also suggested that he could help improve Geralt's image through his music, though Geralt was not receptive.

While they hunted for the "devil", Jaskier told Geralt that the region they were walking through had formerly been part of land belonging to the elves, then known as Dol Blathana, before they had abandoned the valley for palaces in the mountains; Geralt told Jaskier that whatever they were hunting wasn't a devil, as they don't exist. Their conversation was interrupted when they were attacked by the real creature, a Sylvan named Torque. Wanting to be left alone, he charged at Geralt, knocking him to the ground. Geralt got back to his feet and grabbed him by the horns (which were responsible for the title the town had given him), slamming him to the ground. To Geralt's surprise, the creature could talk. Rather than killing Torque, Geralt showed mercy, allowing him to live so long as he left Posada. However, before Geralt and Jaskier could leave the Sylvan behind, someone snuck up behind Geralt and knocked him out.

Geralt woke up in a cave, tied up back-to-back with Jaskier and surrounded by elves. Geralt and Jaskier were repeatedly threatened and beaten by a sickly elf named Toruviel, and Geralt waited until she was close enough to headbutt her. They were joined by Torque and the king of the elves, Filavandrel. Torque had been stealing goods for the elves in the cave ever since they were forced out of Dol Blathanna; this came as a surprise to Jaskier, as it challenged his assumption that the elves had willingly left, when in reality, they had retreated from persecution to caves, not palaces. Filavandrel regretfully told Geralt and Jaskier that he could not allow either of them to leave the cave for fear that they could reveal it was them who had been stealing from the nearby humans, who would then be given a reason to attack the elves again, undoubtedly resulting in casualties on both sides.


Geralt cautioned Filavandrel against killing him and Jaskier in the name of it being the lesser of two evils, comparing Filavandrel's position in that moment to his own in Blaviken and warning him that making decisions in that way would one day be his destruction. Filavandrel protested that the choices he was making were the result of what humans had done to him and his kind: his elders had worked constructively with humans, only to be robbed of all they had. When they fought back, they had been slaughtered in a battle that would come to be known as the "Great Cleansing". Bringing his people down from the mountains, as Geralt suggested, would mean bowing down to the humans, who would make them slaves. Hearing that, Geralt advised them to rebuild elsewhere and explained how, although he sympathized with the elves as someone humans often feared and hated, he had learned that the only way to survive was to coexist with them. Filavandrel then had a change of heart in light of Torque pointing out that Geralt letting the sylvan live confirmed that he was more like him and the elves than humans. 

Geralt and Jaskier left the mountains after being released by Filavandrel. In return, Geralt gave Torque and the elves the 150 ducats he was paid to kill Torque. Jaskier walked down the mountain with Geralt and began to write a tune about Geralt's heroics—designed to help improve his public image like Jaskier had promised—while Geralt followed alongside, protesting that Jaskier's song was exaggerating and misrepresented their encounter with the elves.[2]

### Hunt for the Striga[]

### Hunt for the Striga[]

Three years later, Geralt was in a brothel, where had just finished having sex with a prostitute who had heard the tales of his adventures from Jaskier when she began attempting to match each of his scars with a different conquest. He simply ignored her. Eventually, she informed him that another witcher by the name of Remus had passed through the brothel last month on his way to Temeria, which was plagued by some kind of vicious creature. A few Temerian miners had rounded up 3,000 orens to have the creature killed, and Remus supposedly took the coins and ran. Low on funds to pay for the room he'd been in, Geralt left Roach behind as he left the brothel and set out for Temeria to find Remus.

Geralt arrived in Temeria and listened in on a meeting of the disgruntled miners. When he spoke up and offered to kill their monster, they accused him of trying to steal from them, as Remus had. Geralt informed them that, unlike Remus, he would take payment only after the job was completed and would charge a third of the previous price. He also extended an apology on Remus' behalf as another witcher. The courtier in the court of King Foltest, Lord Ostrit, then arrived with several of his soldiers, demanding that the miners disperse in exchange for him not charging them with treason in light of the things they'd said about rebelling against the king in response to his inaction regarding the monster. As for Geralt, Ostrit ordered his men to see him out of Temeria.

As Geralt and Ostrit's soldiers neared Temeria's border, the guardsmen suddenly fell off their horses and onto the ground. A sorceress by the name of Triss Merigold, a royal advisor of Temeria, revealed herself to Geralt and offered to hire him to kill the mysterious monster after all. She admitted to him that she served King Foltest but was acting under her own agenda without his knowledge. Rather than kill the beast, she wanted Geralt's help in saving it.

Six years before, stable hands had started vanishing from King Foltest's castle. Before long, citizens began disappearing across Temeria. It soon became apparent that the creature was coming from the crypt where the king's sister Adda had been laid to rest. Rumor had it that she was having an affair with a young man in town when she died and that she was with child. If that were true, that child would be the sole heir to the Temerian throne after Foltest never married. When the disappearances in the kingdom had started becoming more frequent, the king had fled to his winter castle, ignoring the rising death toll. As a result, Triss had been sent there three months ago by the Brotherhood of Sorcerers to kill the creature.

Geralt initially believed the creature to be a monster called a vukodlak, but Triss informed him otherwise. She took him to the tomb the creature had emerged from to examine the corpses of those killed by the creature. He examined Remus' corpse, which was among them, and concluded that Triss had covered up his death from the miners to hide the fact that the creature was powerful enough to best a witcher. Upon further examination, Geralt discovered that Remus was missing both his heart and liver; only a striga's eating habits are that selective. He informed Triss that they're very rare and can only be created through a curse, meaning someone must have wanted Adda dead. However, the curse hadn't stopped with Adda, and it turned her daughter into a monster, meaning that the striga was the princess of Temeria.

Triss Merigold presented Geralt to King Foltest, Lord Ostrit, and Captain Segelin, with whom she pleaded to enlist in Geralt's help in stopping the striga's killing. However, Segelin was skeptical of Geralt's claims that Princess Adda was murdered. Triss hoped that the king would allow her to search the abandoned castle for clues as to who killed her, but Segelin protested, fearing that Geralt would kill the princess for the reward he'd been offered. Geralt explained that the striga had grown inside of Adda's corpse, feeding on her womb and mutating for years until she'd gotten so hungry that she was forced to leave and start hunting the king's subjects to emphasize how important it was that the king not continue to do nothing about the monster. The king then grew tired of Geralt and Triss' claims and commanded that everyone leave the chamber.

As everyone exited, Geralt pushed Segelin out last and locked the door behind him, staying in the room with Foltest. Alone with the king, Geralt asked Foltest who had fathered Adda's daughter and questioned why he had never married and fathered an heir. He also pointed out that Foltest, having done nothing up to that point to stop the striga, implied to Geralt that he was really the striga's father. In response, Foltest surmised that the widespread rumors of witchers being devoid of heart and emotion must be true for Geralt not to feel guilty about accusing him of incestuous affairs with his sister while simultaneously campaigning that he kill his own daughter, in Geralt's mind. At that, the guards broke through the door, and Foltest ordered Geralt to leave Temeria.

Instead, Geralt hid outside Foltest's abandoned castle, where Triss found him and asked if he was going to kill the striga after all. Geralt said he was not, but refused to tell her why he cared to help, beyond saying it wasn't for any money he might receive. He then scared away the castle's guards, nervous over what the striga had once done there, and he and Triss entered. Inside, they moved past the remains of the striga's past victims and discovered letters from the former queen of Temeria (Foltest's mother and his sister's mother) in Adda's bedroom. The letter detailed Queen Sancia knew of her children's incestuous relationship and urged them to end it and abort their daughter, confirming Geralt's assumption about the striga's parentage.


Geralt and Triss took this discovery to Ostrit, suspecting that the former queen might have cursed her children. Ostrit dismissed this possibility and revealed that he was close to Adda, serving as her confidant and protector. In light of Sancia's letters, Ostrit suggested that Foltest might have raped Adda and cursed their daughter to cover it up. However, Geralt questioned Ostrit's theory, as he knew Ostrit was downplaying his attachment to Adda, his heightened witcher senses having allowed him to smell Ostrit's scent, old and new, all over Adda's sheets. Under pressure, Ostrit confessed to being Adda's lover and the one responsible for having placed the curse on her, albeit unintentionally, as it had been meant for Foltest, intending to make him suffer, since Ostrit was jealous due his relationship. But Triss is horrified that Ostrit cursed the woman he loved, blaming him for the countless deaths for his jealousy. She even questioned why he didn't simply expose their affair, to which Ostrit pointed out that it would have hurt Adda. Geralt asked how to lift the curse, but Ostrit refused to tell him, as he wanted to see Foltest punished for defiling Adda. In response, Geralt simply knocked him out with a single punch. 

Later, Foltest met Geralt at the entrance to the abandoned castle, where the striga lay. No longer bothering to deny that the monster was his and Adda's daughter, Foltest asked if Geralt would really be able to save her. Geralt honestly answered that he didn't know, and if she were cured, she would be profoundly affected by her time as a striga, as all she'd ever known her entire life until that point was rage and hunger. Geralt then gave Foltest a gift to give his daughter in case the curse was successfully lifted or Geralt couldn't survive his encounter with her. Before leaving Geralt, Foltest claimed that both he and Adda had initially tried to resist their urges, but what they felt for each other was too powerful; in light of that, he envied the fact that he believed Geralt's mutation made him unable to love.

Within the castle, Geralt tied Ostrit to Adda's bed. Once again, he asked Ostrit how to lift the curse on the striga, but Ostrit refused, demanding that Foltest pay for what he had done. However, when he realized that the striga would likely kill him in his current position if the curse remained intact, Ostrit reluctantly revealed that a powerful witch had sold him a lamb and told him to wait until the full moon rose to kill it. Then, he had recited an elven chant and bathed in the lamb's blood until sunrise when a rooster crowed three times. Geralt realized in light of this information that the only way to cure the princess was to keep her out of her crypt until sunrise.

When the striga rose from its crypt, Geralt left Ostrit, still tied to the bed, behind to look for it. The striga approached Ostrit in Geralt's absence, and Ostrit begged it for his life, claiming to have loved Adda and not meant for her or the striga to be the ones who were cursed. Ignoring his pleas, the striga killed him.

Geralt came face-to-face with the creature, hideous and hunched, with a severed umbilical cord still attached and dragging on the ground as it walked. He tried to entrap it with silver chains, but to no avail; the striga broke free. A fight ensued between Geralt and the striga, which ultimately resulted in the creature being knocked unconscious. While the striga was down, Geralt placed a barrier over the entrance to the castle, preventing it from leaving. When the striga ran for it, the barrier knocked it back, and Geralt put on some brass knuckles and knocked the striga to the ground. As the sun rose, both he and the striga raced for the crypt. Geralt arrived there first and sealed himself inside to block the striga from accessing it.

When the sun rose, the curse lifted, and the striga transformed into an adolescent girl, Geralt having saved her life as he had been unable to with Renfri, the last princess he'd encountered, who had been turned into a monster. Geralt slowly approached as she lay on the ground, but she abruptly lunged at him and sliced at his throat with her nails and teeth. He bit her neck to get her off of him, drawing blood, and passed out as blood poured from his wound.

Geralt awakened shortly after, having been healed by Triss. She informed him that the princess would heal from the wound he'd inflicted and that King Foltest had issued a statement decreeing that Lord Ostrit had given his life defeating the creature. The miners were therefore building a statue in his honor. Triss then asked Geralt about Renfri, whose name he had uttered while he was asleep. He didn't reply and simply asked for his money, which he'd earned for saving the princess. Triss skeptically asked him if all life meant to him was monsters and money, and he confirmed that it was. Triss didn't believe that and informed him that there's a vortex of fate around every person that draws their destiny closer with each decision they make. Triss then handed him his money and returned the gift he had left for the princess: Renfri's brooch. Before they parted, she told Geralt that she felt that something was waiting for him out in the world. Something more.[3]

### Royal Betrothal[]


In 1249, Geralt entered a tavern covered in the entrails of a selkiemore he had just killed, interrupting a townsperson's story of how the creature had swallowed Geralt whole. Jaskier started to sing a tune in favor of Geralt, and the townspeople in the tavern joined in, celebrating Geralt's victorious battle against the beast. Jaskier pointed out how his songs had done what he'd said they would, spreading Geralt's reputation as a monster slayer, and asked Geralt for a favor: in exchange for acting as his bodyguard while he performed at the betrothal banquet for the princess of Cintra, Geralt would be able to enjoy a night of food, women, and wine. Jaskier required protection while attending the event, as every significant lord, knight, and king from the surrounding lands would be in attendance, many of whom he'd personally crossed, having had affairs with their lovers. Geralt begrudgingly agreed, though he protested Jaskier's claim that they were friends, insisting he needed no one and didn't want anyone needing him. He also emphasized that, although he would keep Jaskier alive for the night, he would remain neutral and not intervene in disputes among humans. During their conversation, Jaskier questioned what happens to witchers as they age, and Geralt explained that there is no retirement for his kind: they hunt monsters until they get too old to win anymore and something kills them, and he wanted nothing more than that for himself. 


When Geralt and Jaskier arrived at the Cintran castle, Geralt was immediately recognized by an old associate of his, Mousesack, despite Jaskier's hope that Geralt would remain unnoticed and his presence wouldn't draw too much attention to them. Mousesack warned Geralt that the event would likely last all night until dawn, as every potential suitor in attendance from near and far was vying for Princess Pavetta's hand. Mousesack informed Geralt that the ceremony was rigged; however, Crach an Craite, unbeknownst to most, was already set to marry Pavetta. Her mother, Queen Calanthe, the Lioness, had already arranged it with Craite's uncle, Eist Tuirseach, whose own marriage proposals to Queen had previously been refused three times according to Mousesack. Leaving Mousesack, Geralt came to Jaskier's defense as he was being interrogated by a nobleman who believed he'd once caught Jaskier having an affair with his wife. Geralt lied to the man, claiming that Jaskier was " kicked in the balls by an Ox as a child" and therefore couldn't be the man he thought Jaskier was, which diffused the situation. 

As the feast progressed, Geralt bore witness as Crach and another guest got into an argument, both claiming to have defeated manticores. When Queen Calanthe asked Geralt to settle the dispute as an expert on monsters, he initially claimed that they were both lying, as their descriptions of the creatures they'd killed didn't match that of a manticore. Still, to prevent a fight from ensuing, he suggested that they might have encountered a subspecies that he was unfamiliar with. Intrigued by Geralt, Queen Calanthe inquired about his encounter with Filavandrel and the elves, which the court was familiar with because of Jaskier's songs. Geralt explained that, contrary to what Jaskier had written, he'd gotten his ass kicked and was about to have his throat cut when Filavandrel spared his life. Queen Calanthe admired Geralt's willingness to paint himself in the shadow of his failures, as she put it, and invited him to take a seat beside her.

Queen Calanthe enquired about Geralt's presence at the feast, and he explained that he was there to protect Jaskier from vengeful cuckolds. Despite his saying that he was not interested in being hired by anyone else, she explained that she hoped that should chaos ensue during the night that she would be able to count on him to use it as an excuse to "strategically remove" individuals from the court that she could not take on herself in the interest of the fairness and decorum that being queen demanded of her. Once again, Geralt insisted on not picking a side in a dispute between humans and continued to refuse to help her.

Later, Queen Calanthe questioned why there are so few witchers remaining. Geralt explained that since the sacking of Kaer Morhen, it is no longer possible to create more of them. Geralt asked why she regularly risked her life on the battlefield when she could instead rest on her throne, and Queen Calanthe replied that fighting was simple compared to life at court. Just as Crach was about to propose to Pavetta, a stranger, Lord Urcheon of Erlenwald, known as "Duny," then interrupted the ceremony, his face hidden under a knight's armor. He'd come to claim Pavetta's hand in marriage. Eist ripped Duny's helmet off where he knelt before Calanthe's throne, revealing a monstrous face resembling that of a hedgehog, shocking the court.

Queen Calanthe demanded that Geralt kill him, but he refused, as Urcheon was no monster: his appearance had been caused by a curse placed on him. Queen Calanthe ordered her guards to slay Urcheon instead. Urcheon disarmed the guards and explained to Queen Calanthe that Pavetta belonged to him because he'd claimed the Law of Surprise. More of the queen's guards entered, and they attacked Urcheon. Geralt came to his defense, along with Eist, who had turned to their side at the mention of the Law of Surprise. Together, they dispatched Queen Calanthe's guards with little difficulty, and an even larger fight then ensued between the guests of the banquet as the tensions that had been brewing all night came to a head, as Calanthe had predicted it eventually would.


Queen Calanthe stood in the centre of the room and commanded the fighting to end. When it did, Pavetta ran to Urcheon and reminded him that she had told him to stay away from the banquet, revealing that Duny, as she called him, was Pavetta's secret lover. As Geralt and the rest of the party's guests listened, Duny addressed Calanthe and explained that his appearance was the result of a curse, as Geralt had correctly deduced. He continued to explain that many years before, when he had saved the life of Queen Calanthe's late husband, King Roegner, he had chosen the Law of Surprise—an old tradition entitling someone to the first good thing the person they claimed it from was surprised with—as payment. Roegner had returned home from the battle they'd fought to find that Calanthe was pregnant with Pavetta, meaning that she was what Duny would be entitled to. Revealing she was already aware of this by the time of the banquet, Queen Calanthe expressed her fury with the situation they were now in, and Geralt realized that that was what had motivated her earlier attempt at convincing him to kill Duny. 


In an attempt to convince Calanthe to allow his and Pavetta's engagement, Duny told her that although he had not initially intended ever even to approach Pavetta directly, he'd watched her from afar, and destiny had eventually intervened, the two falling in love despite his curse. Both Eist and Mousesack took his side and advised Queen Calanthe to honor the Law of Surprise, concerned that dire consequences could result if destiny and tradition were subverted. Although Geralt didn't believe in destiny as they did, he agreed that a promise made is a promise to be honored and encouraged Queen Calanthe to listen to them. Queen Calanthe seemed to accept this, handing over her sword and extending her hand to Duny, until she pulled him close, revealed that she had no intention of cowering to destiny or traditions upheld by men who did not understand her mother's love for Pavetta, and abruptly aimed a knife at Duny's throat. Pavetta screamed out, her latent magical abilities awakening, and sent Geralt and the other guests of the banquet flying across the room. Pavetta's magic summoned powerful winds that raged through the hall hard enough to lift her and Duny to float above the others until Geralt used magic to knock them down and break the trance Pavetta seemed to be in. 

In light of Pavetta's reaction to the threat against Duny, Calanthe finally broke down and announced that she would no longer stand in the way of destiny or the couple's marriage. As queen, Calanthe then married Pavetta and Duny there on the spot, and as the two kissed, it was revealed that the fulfillment of Pavetta and Duny's entwined destinies was the cure to Duny's curse. His distorted features reverted back to those of a normal man. Elated, he turned to Geralt and wanted to repay him for saving his life. Geralt initially declined, but Duny insisted that he be adequately repaid so that he could continue his newly curse-free life unencumbered by a debt to him.

Wishing to placate Duny and leave the hall, Geralt chose to make them even by taking Duny's own lead and claiming the Law of Surprise himself. Responding to Calanthe's protests, he made it clear that he didn't intend to invoke this or lay claim to whatever surprise Duny received. However, moments later, Pavetta suddenly threw up, surprising Duny (and the rest of the room) with the fact that she was likely pregnant. Disturbed, Geralt abruptly left, making it clear that he had meant it when he'd said he did not intend to act on the Law of Surprise.

Mousesack, intending to stay in Queen Calanthe's court and help Pavetta develop her powerful magical abilities, tried to convince Geralt to stay as well. He pointed out that whether he liked it or not, Geralt was now bound to the family, and he advised against trying to outrun destiny. Geralt, however, reiterated that he didn't believe in destiny. Mousesack believed that the bond that would form between Geralt and Pavetta's unborn child would be extraordinary. If he dismissed it and left without claiming the child, surprise, Mousesack worried that he would unleash true calamity upon them all. Geralt was unconvinced and decided to take his chances, leaving Cintra without any intention of ever coming back.[4]

### Three Wishes from a Djinn[]

### Three Wishes from a Djinn[]

A decade after the royal betrothal, Jaskier found Geralt at the edge of a lake, fishing for a djinn that was rumored to be buried at the bottom. Geralt was hoping to use the wishes it would grant to cure severe insomnia, and Jaskier concluded that his sleeplessness was likely related to what Mousesack had said to him about the Law of Surprise and the consequences that could come from Geralt's failing to claim Princess Pavetta's child. However, Geralt emphatically denied this possibility and lashed out at Jaskier for the suggestion, insulting him by comparing his singing to a disappointing, filling-less pie.

As Jaskier protested this, Geralt pulled a bottle inscribed with a mage's seal from the water, and the djinn trapped inside. Jaskier wrestled with Geralt for control of the bottle, demanding that Geralt apologize before he would hand it over, and, in the process, unintentionally broke the bottle's seal, releasing the djinn. Jaskier rapidly made two petty wishes before Geralt stopped him and reminded him that there were only three. The argument between the two escalated until Geralt exclaimed that he just wanted some peace, and Jaskier threw the bottle to the ground, shattering it. As Geralt frantically gathered the broken pieces, trying to salvage them, the djinn attacked Jaskier's throat. Geralt managed to scare it away with Aard, but not before Jaskier began to cough up blood.

Geralt pulled Jaskier onto Roach's back and rushed him to the elf healer Chireadan in the nearby city of Rinde, who informed them that Jaskier's affliction was magical in nature. Untreated, the damage to his throat would rapidly continue to worsen, and unless it was stopped quickly, the magic's effects may become irreversible, eventually resulting in death. The medicine given by the healer would provide Jaskier with a few more hours. He advised that Geralt take Jaskier to another town for help, despite the urgency of his injury, as the only mage in close proximity was extremely dangerous and extremely cunning. Geralt disregarded Chireadan's advice and set off in search of this malicious mage, said to be imprisoned in the mayor's house.


That night, Geralt and Jaskier broke into the mayor's house to find him under some trance, naked and rambling. Realizing that the mayor would not be any help, Geralt, with Jaskier, they walked further into the house and stumbled upon a massive orgy made up of the town's citizens, magically orchestrated by Yennefer of Vengerberg, the powerful mage Chireadan had warned about. Dropping off Jaskier with a couple of the women, Geralt approached the masked sorceress, who sat at the back of the room, and he introduces himself to her by bringing her a jug of apple juice, a request from the mayor. The mage, seeing that Geralt was immune to her spell, correctly deduced not only that he was a mutant but that he was the famous White Wolf. Yennefer has never seen a witcher up close before and expresses professional curiosity about him. Geralt is shown clearly amazed by Yennefer's beauty, while both they are intrigued by one another. However, Jaskier's condition is worsening quickly, and Geralt pulled her attention to the spell the djinn had cast on him by promising to indulge her curiosity about him for as long as she liked if she helped him—and to pay her well. Seeing the seal on the djinn's bottle, Yennefer agreed to his terms and broke the spell, dehypnotizing the orgy participants, seemingly bewildered by their surroundings. 

Yennefer put Jaskier in a deep healing sleep. She explained that he would be asleep long enough for Geralt to bathe, which Yennefer insisted he needed, as she was able to determine his horse's breed from smelling it on him. While Geralt bathed, she made a point that fishing for a djinn is an extreme remedy for sleeplessness. Geralt replied that he was desperate, although his concern for Jaskier in the wake of the djinn's attack had taken precedence over that.


Yennefer undressed, sat back-to-back with Geralt in the bathtub, and began to question him as he had promised her she would be able if she helped Jaskier, asking if all witchers are as blessed as he is, being as they're made from magic. However, as Geralt explained, being a witcher hadn't made for a happy childhood, and "blessed" was the wrong word to use to describe them. Judging by Yennefer's scars on her wrists from a suicide attempt and her wit as they spoke, he could tell she hadn't had much of a happy childhood either. Verbally sparring together, he accused her of capitalizing on the political situation in Rinde for her own profit. However, Yennefer claimed that she was more concerned with serving the stifled townspeople. Ultimately, they both knew there was more to the other's claims about their motivations—Geralt looking for the djinn purely to help himself sleep and Yennefer simply wanting to help the repressed people of Rinde—than they were revealing. Although Geralt had offered to pay her whatever amount she named for helping Jaskier, Yennefer decided that his company and conversation that night were payment enough for her services, much to his chagrin. 

Geralt watched over Jaskier as he slept, not yet fully trusting Yennefer. Although he wouldn't admit aloud that they were friends, Geralt confessed that he regretted what he had said during his argument with Jaskier over the djinn's bottle, and he did not want it to be the last thing Jaskier remembered. Yennefer assured Geralt that Jaskier would survive and recover his vocal talents. Geralt looked around and realized that Yennefer was planning to trap the djinn, but before he could leave with Jaskier, Yennefer cautioned him against it, as Jaskier would die without her help. Using this as leverage, she explained that the djinn was tied to its master, and as Jaskier had only made two wishes, Yennefer needed him to make his third so that she could capture it for herself when it was released from him. Geralt, overtaken by the sudden smell of lilac and gooseberries, realized that Yennefer had full control of him, and he blacked out just as she kissed him.


Groggy, Geralt awakened in a cell with Chireadan after an apparent rampage through Rinde. Although he couldn't recall much of it, he had allegedly attacked a pawnbroker and an apothecary, both of whom were threatening Yennefer's position in town by serving on the town council and planning to usurp the mayor and kick Yennefer out of Rinde. Yennefer had used magic to force Geralt to enact revenge on her behalf, and although Chireadan had tried to stop him, the guards who were there to arrest Geralt assumed he was there to help him and had taken him into custody as well. Noting that Geralt was to be sentenced by the same council members he had attacked, Chireadan informed him that they would almost certainly put him to death. Chireadan chastised Geralt for going to see Yennefer despite his warnings, although he admitted that he could've better prepared Geralt, who questioned if Chireadan was under her spell as well. He denied being under a spell cast by Yennefer, instead conceding that he was in love with her, and he suspected Geralt might be in the same position. 

A guard, whom Geralt recognize as the same one he had beaten up the night before on his way into the mayor's home—entered and began to attack him, confirming Chireadan's assumption that they had been sentenced to death. As he prepared to finish Geralt off, Geralt made a wish that the guard would "burst," and he did just that, his head exploding. As it turned out, Geralt was the one with the wishes, not Jaskier, and had now used two of the three, the first having been what had harmed Jaskier, as Geralt had said he wanted peace from Jaskier.

Geralt hurriedly made his escape and rushed off to find Jaskier and Yennefer, arriving just as Jaskier was exiting the mayor's home. Geralt realized from Jaskier that Yennefer was trying to become the djinn's vessel to gain more power and rushed inside to prevent her from accidentally killing herself by doing it. Jaskier tried to persuade Geralt not to risk his life for Yennefer. But Geralt explained that Yennefer had saved Jaskier's life, so he couldn't let her die.

Entering the building, Geralt found Yennefer struggling to contain the djinn. It was getting stronger because it was Geralt who truly held the wishes, and it was neither unbound nor weakened when Jaskier made a wish at Yennefer's demand. Geralt offered to make whatever wish Yennefer wanted on her behalf so long as she stopped endangering herself by trying to contain the djinn, fearing that Yennefer becoming a vessel for it would be too much for her to control successfully. Yennefer refused his help, becoming unstable as she continued to struggle with the djinn. With the djinn's power raging, the tower they were in started to collapse around them. To save Yennefer, Geralt made his final wish, and the djinn was freed. The building then caved in on both of them as it fled.

Before the falling debris could crush them as the section of the building they were in collapsed, Yennefer managed to portal herself and Geralt downstairs. She lashed out at him and blamed him for the djinn's escape and the mayhem it would surely wreak now that it wasn't contained. Geralt refused to feel guilty about releasing the djinn, however, as he had saved her life (just as she had his), and stated that djinn are only dark creatures when they're held captive, meaning he was certain that it wouldn't cause much harm now that it was free. The two continued to accuse each other of ruining everything... and then suddenly, Geralt and Yennefer gave into their attraction together and proceeded to have passionate sex there in the building. Outside, Chireadan and Jaskier couldn't help notice that they were alive, "Really alive!" as Jaskier remarked. Afterwards, Yennefer asked him what his last wish was, but Geralt had already fallen asleep. 

### Prevent the war between land and sea[]


Some time after Geralt and Yennefer's djinn encounter, Geralt, accompanied by Jaskier, finds themselves near ​​the coastal city of Bremervoord at night. They are tracking a monster, an Allamorax, a massive, rare aquatic creature which Geralt has only seen in books. During the hunt on the treacherous, Geralt warns Jaskier to stay safe due to treacherous, rocky terrain, since his boots are useless for climbing rocks. Suddenly, Geralt sensed the Allamorax beneath him, hidden from beneath the rocks, moving to attack Jaskier. Geralt saves him while he goes into hiding and battles the Allamorax, ultimately dragging the witcher into the water with it. After a long battle, Geralt subdues the creature in a watery cave. But then a pair of merpeople appear and beg Geralt to spare the creature. They inform him that the Allamorax is not actually inherently dangerous to humans. It was only looking for oysters and pearls to sustenance, but he doesn't eat humans. Its only crime is being hungry. Speaking in the merpeople language, Geralt realizing Allamorax is misunderstood and not a mindless threat, choosing not to kill it for the pearl divers who hired him. He then asks the merpeople to take him back to the shore. 


In a tavern, Jaskier is frustrated and complains, and isn't very happy with Geralt, as they're broke or to afford food because Geralt spared the creature, accusing him of having a "moral code" that often leaves them with no money. Geralt maintains his stance, explaining that he could not kill the Allamorax because it was innocent. But Jaskier also criticizes him of following the raven-haired sorceress's influence. Geralt explains that although he follows a "moral code", they'll soon find a way to get money. Even if it's not in Bremervoord. But Jaskier reminds him that they came to this town to avoid running into Yennefer, which irritates Geralt when mentioned her. At that moment, he thought of Yennefer and their relationship between them, which dates back to the during the period where Geralt and Yennefer have had multiple separations, reunions, and nice nights together since the djinn, even though they grew apart due to the pain of one always leaving the other alone wherever they had met before dawn. 


As Jaskier continued to complain, he and Geralt are mocked by the tavern's patrons and the bartender, who mock Geralt for being a "witcher who doesn't kill monsters," specifically citing a recent incident where he let the Allamorax go, leading to them being thrown out. were thrown out. Outside, they were approached by a spice merchant named Teleri Drouhard, who recognized Jaskier as the famous composer from Oxenfurt, and offered him the chance to perform at a royal banquet of the king. Accepting this offer in exchange for a good payment, Geralt and Jaskier went to the kingdom. There at the royal banquet, while Jaskier was preparing for his show, he unexpectedly ran into an old friend of his, Essi Daven. Essi greeted Jaskier as "Julian" and Jaskier greeted her as "Little Eye", revealing that she herself had arranged for Drouhard to hire him. Jaskier then introduced Essi to Geralt. Geralt asked how they knew each other, to which Essi explained that they both grew up in Bremervoord, which confused Geralt, due he believed Jaskier was from Oxenfurt. Jaskier then revealed that he had indeed grown up in Bremervoord, that his real name was Julian, and that Zelest, the king's bastard son, and other children bullied him as a child for his preference for music over weapons. He hadn't thought about it since leaving his hometown and change his name. 

The arrival of King Usveldt and his son, Prince Agloval, is announced. To Jaskier's dismay, he sees and recognizes Zelest among them, now as the stern military leader for King Usveldt. Meanwhile, Geralt suddenly notices that there is the residents are unhappy toward the prince. Essi explains them that they are fed up because there have been five attacks on pearl divers in near by waters in the last few months, and the king has taken no action to stop the attacks. Although a sea monster, even the Allamorax, is officially blamed, the locals believe that the attacks are perpetrated by the merpeople, who are known for being extremely territorial. The royalty has remained aloof from the conflict, given that the prince is known to be in love with a mermaid.


The celebration continues, and Essi is taken aside by her nephew to dance with her family. Geralt go outside for a beer, reflecting on what he has just heard. Outside the celebratory banquet, as he watches the fireworks, he is approached by Essi, who shows great curiosity about him, having heard many stories about his exploits, as described in Jaskier's ballads. She says that in one tells of Geralt fighting unarmed a werewolf in Moulderwood under the full moon. However, Geralt, with dry humor, replies that he didn't fight it at all, he cured it with an enchanted medicinal herb. Another ballad tells of him defeating a horde of vampires, and Geralt reveals it was actually only one vampire, and he used a simple stake rather than an elaborate fight, contrary to Jaskier's poetic descriptions, because he tends to exaggerate events. The conversation continued lightly until Essi mentioned the other ballad, but no less important, is the djinn, about Geralt saving the life of a beautiful sorceress and how they became intertwined. Upon hearing this, Geralt fell silent for a long time. Essi changed the subject, talking about Jaskier, explaining that she understood why he left. In the town, they expected all men to follow the tradition of being sailors, but Jaskier had always been creative and different. Geralt asked why he called her "Little Eye" when Essi had such large eyes, interpreting this response as a flirtatious remark that Geralt quickly regrets. Taken aback by this, Essi, displaying her wit, jokes about his lack of flirting skills, recognizing that his affections lie elsewhere. 

Jaskier arrives and boasts about his performance, which has just ended, pleased with the enthusiastic applause he received. He also announces the next bard to sing, who turns out to be Essi. She reveals that she is the local bard they had mentioned at the banquet. As soon as Essi begins to sing, her voice surprises and captivates everyone present. Jaskier, listening attentively to the melody, soon recognizes that she is singing his song from before. Without hesitation, he joins her on stage.


As the performance was underway, Geralt overheared General Zelest talking to Drouhard, who suggested eliminating the merpeople, but Zelest claimed they can't take such drastic measures because of Agloval's infatuation with one, though he suspects the merpeople have bewitched him. Geralt intervenes, remarking that humans can be even more manipulative. His words spark a tense confrontation between them. At that moment, the arrival of a princess from another kingdom is announced, a potential suitor for Agloval, capturing everyone's attention. Princess Nispen of Maribor arrives majestically, bearing gifts for the prince. Suddenly, Geralt's attention was drawn by the vibration of his medallion, alerting him to some nearby danger. A mortally wounded diver disrupts the banquet, claiming to the king that he and other divers had been attacked on their ship by those "fish fucks", the vodnik, after which he died at the spot. Convinced that the merpeople were responsible, the outraged counts demanded that the king declare war on them. Under pressure, King Usveldt decide to act. But Zelest warnd that a monster is lurking off the kingdom's shores and points the finger at the monster hunter at the banquet. Upon hearing this, Agloval suggests hiring Geralt to investigate, discover the threat, and find and kill the culprit. Zelest believes that if the witcher confirm the merpeople are behind the attacks, the only option would be to declare war. Although Geralt reluctantly agrees the job, he wouldn't help justify a war, but Jaskier suggested that it might help prevent it. 


Camping in a woods, Geralt and Jaskier eat a roasted animal Geralt has prepared. They discuss about how Jaskier never mentioned being from Bremervoord, especially since he knows Geralt isn't from Rivia. Jaskier admits he left his town to escape its restrictive atmosphere and become the person he wanted to be. Geralt points out that his friend Essi doesn't fit that description, to which Jaskier agreed, adding that she's like a sister to him. Jaskier then try to steer the conversation away by mentioning Geralt's possible attraction to Essi, as he hinted that there was a spark between them. He realized he liked her. Geralt simply denies it, stating that he is only need coin, peace, and quiet. Furthermore, Jaskier argues that she's a good woman before comparing her to Yennefer, referring to her as a "raven-haired, sunken-eyed, serpent-tongued she-demon." Jaskier joked that despite Geralt's tough exterior, he has a "soft heart of a child". Visibly uncomfortable, Geralt suggests they rest for tomorrow's mission. Before leaving, Jaskier encourages him to be more open with others. 

That night, Geralt falls into a dream where, in a serene water-side setting, dream of a romantic moment with Essi. The dream shifting to Yennefer. Yennefer wakes him in the dream, and when he jolts awake in the morning, Geralt immediately dodges a surprise attack from a vodnik that has ambushed them. He and the vodnik engage in a fight, while Jaskier remains asleep, oblivious to the fight. Geralt drinks one of his elixirs, gaining the upper hand, disarming and wounding the sea creature, but the vodnik uses a powerful blast to escape just then Jaskier woke.


As they track the sea creature by following his trail of blood left, Jaskier criticizes Geralt's decision to spare a creature that nearly killed him. Geralt explains that he let it go because it's more useful alive than dead, as tracking it will lead them to the lair and the rest of them. Geralt identifies the creature as a vodnik and knows that they are group hunters. He deduces that a single vodnik wouldn't have been capable for the coordinated attack on the ship alone and Geralt wonders how that vodnik found them, or if the Allamorax and the merpeople he let go earlier spread the word about what happened, leading the vodnik's attack on him. At that very moment, Geralt senses someone following them and draws his sword, only to realize it's Essi. Essi offered to help them and wants to do something about the war. Although Geralt appreciate her willingness, they needs a boat to follow the vodnik. With knowledge of the terrain, Essi reports that they can take advantage of the low tide and advance on foot without problems to the Dragons Fangs. 


Geralt, Jaskier, and Essi arrive at the Dragon Fangs, a place Jaskier explains always gave him childhood nightmares that place. Geralt find the lair of the vodniks, where sees the same vodnik badly wounded. He quickly runs after him, pinning him to the ground. Geralt confront and interrogates him, demanding to know who sent him to kill him. However, the vodnik refuses to answer, claiming that if he does, "she" will kill him. But Geralt even threatens to do it himself if he doesn't. When questioned about whether "she" ordered him to kill the pearl divers, the vodnik denies any responsibility for the attacks on the ships. Suddenly, dozens of vodniks arrive, while Geralt continues to threaten him. He further threatens to prove that he hasn't gone soft on killing monsters unless the creature talks. But before the vodnik can name the woman, Zelest and his forces arrive. Zelest shoots the vodnik with a spear, killing him, and declares he is doing the witcher's work, since Geralt hasn't finished off these creatures. A fight breaks out, and Geralt accuses Zelest for intentionally instigating a war when he is trying to prevent one. Tensions escalate, and the vodniks attack Zelest's soldiers. Merpeople emerge from the water, joining the fight, and a fierce battle erupts. Heavy casualties ensue, and amidst the chaos, Zelest mortally wounds the merman Geralt had encountered earlier in the cave and intervenes, sending a Sign against Zelest. In a moment of inattention, Essi is attacked and dragged by a vodnik into the water. Geralt manages to rescue her from drowning. As casualties mount, Geralt halts the fight and threatens Zelest, warning him to retreat or he will kill the only monster he sees. Zelest reluctantly retreats, vowing to complain to the king about Geralt's interference. At the point where the tide begins rise too high, Essi guides them along a path to leave the area. 


Resting to rest at Essi's house for the night, she tends to Geralt's wounds from the fight, as Jaskier suggests they speak directly with the mermaid and the prince to get to the bottom of things and uncover the truth, suspecting manipulation behind the situation. Essi suggests they meet at their meeting place, Founder's Rock, in the morning. Meanwhile, Geralt expresses deep skepticism, about human motives, believing the conflict is merely a pretext to initiate a war of extermination against sea creatures to gain an advantage, rather than for humans seek the truth. In response, Essi suspects the mysterious woman who mentioned the vodnik earlier could be referring to the mermaid queen, theorizing that the mermaid's mother could be involved in the plot to protect her daughter. Geralt muses that love often requires sacrifices that people cannot make, causing more pain than joy. He expresses to Essi his belief that his capacity for love is fleeting, tethered to "The Path" and his inability to abandon his road-bound life. Despite Geralt's emotional barriers, he and Essi grow close, a dynamic immediately noticed by Jaskier. 

At dawn the three of them head straight towards Founder's Rock. While traveling, Essi and Jaskier share a camaraderie rooted about how Jaskier sang to the Countess of Stael, telling the story in song lyrics.


They arrive at the meeting point, where they encounter Agloval and the mermaid Sh'eenaz. Speaking in her language, Geralt directly questions Sh'eenaz about whether her people were responsible in sent the vodnik to kill him. But midway through the conversation, Essi interrupts, correcting Geralt's bluntness and suggests him be more diplomatic. Speaking in an ancient tongue, Sh'eenaz observes that them appear to be lovers, an observation Geralt immediately dismisses, stating he barely knows her. Changing the subject, Agloval asks Essi to translate for Sh'eenaz that he would like to marry her, but it's clear the two disagree on how to make it happen. Essi translates his words to Sh'eenaz, who responds by asking how this would work. Agloval crudely suggests keeping her in a tank of water. Essi immediately condemns this idea, accusing Agloval of wanting to keep Sh'eenaz as a "pet" rather than treating her as a princess and his equal. She also accuses him of demanding Sh'eenaz lose everything, while he is unwilling to sacrifice anything of his own for her, not even a little sacrifice. 

Geralt intervenes in the escalating tensions to address the pearl divers' deaths, suggesting they focus to resolve the underlying conflict to prevent a full-scale war. Essi translates his words to Sh'eenaz, during which Sh'eenaz reveals she denies any knowledge of the vodnik's recent attack on the witcher or her people's attacks on the ships. Following this, Geralt informs Agloval that he was attacked, shortly after being hired, leading him to suspect that someone doesn't want him to discover who killed the pearl divers.

But then the conversation shifts, and a heated argument erupts between the prince and the mermaid. Sh'eenaz gets deeply angered by Agloval's refusal to defend his half brother Zelest from escalating attacks he has launched on her people, specifically his inaction regarding the killing of her cousin. But Agloval, pressured by his father and influenced by his distrustful, warlike advisors, insults Sh'eenaz, suggesting that Zelest might have been right about her "bewitching" him and implies he regrets his love for her. Distraught by the accusation and the betrayal of their love, Sh'eenaz bursts into tears and returns to the sea. As a consequence of this fracture in their relationship removes the last hope for peace, war is officially declared on both sea and land.


However, Geralt, Essi, and Jaskier continued investigating and searched for clues in the wreckage of one of the fishermen's ships. Geralt thanked Essi for her support, speaking her merpeople language fluently. But Essi clarified that she had only come for her nephew, who was being sent to war. Suddenly, Geralt, upon finding the corpse of a diver riddled with spears, make a discovery; he noticed that the spears, while typical of vodnik's weapons, were driven in at an angle that indicates its were thrust only from below. Geralt deduced that the vodnik have legs, but none had boarded the ship to kill the divers, concluding that whoever attacked the ships had done so only from the water, as the attack pattern does not match the behavior of the vodnik, leading him to suspect a different attacker. Inside the wreck, they find a peridot necklace that Essi identifies as belonging to the merpeople royal family. With this, Jaskier confirm Essi's theory and her connection that Queen Dahut might indeed be behind it all. However, knowing the answer, Geralt quickly returns to the castle, where he and Jaskier burst onto the throne before the king and Agloval, interrupting his wedding proposal to Princess Nispen. Geralt challenges Agloval, confronting him for abandoning his love for Sh'eenaz. Geralt avoids arrest by Zelest and his guards by revealing he has discovered the perpetrator of the pearl diver killings, prompting Agloval to request to hear his side of the story. 


The culprits weren't the vodniks. The attack on the ships was orchestrated by a creature that took the form of a kraken to simulate the strength of ten vodniks. Extending the peridot necklace he has found among the shipwreck wreckage, he revealed that the responsible for the attacks was a mermaid from the royal, pointing to a culprit within the merpeople royal family. But Geralt assured that it wasn't Sh'eenaz who had done it, even doubting that she knew. The mermaid he deduces as responsible is Melusina, the sea witch and Sh'eenaz's aunt. She would be the only member of the royal in using magic to shapeshift into a massive kraken to commit the attacks, framing the merpeople. He knew this because he saw her do it when he sensed her presence on the day of the banquet, where she was posing as "Princess Nispen" by vibrating of his witcher medallion, just as it was doing now. Geralt then pointed her out and exposed her, revealing that the sea witch disguised as a princess had been among them all along, which this forced Melusina to reveal herself. Upon being exposed in court, Melusina attacks and killed the guards and fought with Geralt, who managed to wound her, before fleeing back to the sea. As he had deduced, this was from a Jaskier's tale about a plague in the orchards of Maribor. 

Agloval, outraged, exploded at his father, as it has also been revealed that the King Usveldt was involved and has been collaborating with Melusina to orchestrate the attacks on the ships, to sow fear and discord, and ultimately sabotaging Agloval's desire to marry Sh'eenaz. Usveldt attempts to justify these actions as necessary, arguing that he acted to bring Agloval to his senses, but Agloval was furious and horrified to learn his father sacrificed innocent lives. Without hesitation, the king replies that he would do it again if it meant his son would open his eyes, for he never wanted to accept his marriage to the mermaid, refusing to see his family's legacy tarnished or come to an end. Incapable of accepting his father's cruelty, Agloval rejects his willingness to sacrifice his own people to maintain a narrow, traditional legacy.

Determined to continue the conflict, Usveldt orders Zelest to take Geralt and Jaskier to be executed at the Dragon's Fangs. However, aware of the true, Zelest refuses to carry out this injustice perpetrated by a manipulative king, and decides to turn his back on his father, since he initially supported the war because he believed the merpeople were responsible for the attacks. For his defiance, Zelest is arrested alongside the prisoners.


Arriving with the royal fleet at Dragon's Fangs, the king prepared to throw Geralt, Jaskier, and Zelest overboard. He decided to kill Geralt first, but since a witcher fears neither pain nor even death, he chose to kill his friends first. But just then, Zelest leaped backward overboard, giving Geralt the opportunity to attack and free himself and Jaskier. They were surrounded by soldiers when Sh'eenaz arrived and intervened, using powerful magic to halt the king's troops. Sh'eenaz confronts Geralt, demanding to know if Agloval cares about the war he is escalating. Geralt explains that Agloval does love her, and attempts to reveal that her aunt and the king were involved in orchestrating the war. The other fleets fire spears, killing some merpeople, and all-out war broke out between humans and sea creatures. Vodniks board the fleet, and Geralt, Jaskier, and Zelest fight them off. Amidst the battle, Melusina arrives, and using magic, transforming into the enormous kraken, brutally attacking the ship. During the boarding of the fleet, Melusina kills Zelest, ordering the vodniks to deal with the witcher. Geralt quickly dispatches them, with even Jaskier assisting him. Meanwhile, Sh'eenaz is captured by her aunt, but Agloval, persuaded by Essi, arrives to rescue her. However, he is nearly killed by a vodnik, but his father saves him, only for him to push him overboard. Geralt fights his way and frees Sh'eenaz by severing one of the kraken's tentacles. He then engages the kraken in a fierce battle. Although he manages to wound it several times, he loses his sword. King Usveldt injures Sh'eenaz, rendering her unable to swim and nearly causing her to drown but she is healed by her mother, Queen Dahut. Geralt saw Essi being grabbed by a vodnik and went to help her. She cut her hair to free herself, and Geralt eliminated the vodnik. Continuing the battle against the sea witch, Essi throwing his sword, infused with an elixir, at him, and Geralt leaped toward the creature. He fights his way out from the inside, tearing the creature's intestines. He lunged at it and finally stabbed it in the heart to kill Melusina in the process. The ship sinks and Geralt saves Jaskier. 

After the conflict ceases, they meet with Essi and Agloval on a boat, where the prince begins to confront his father about what he has done. Agloval then resolutely declares before everyone that the merpeople are not his enemies, nor are the humans his, as they have been manipulated. He orders the withdrawal of the entire royal fleet, thus halting the war, confident that a solution can be found to achieve peace.

In the of wedding of Agloval and Sh'eenaz, all the merpeople and all from the coastal kingdom attend, Geralt, Essi, and Jaskier included. They marry, and Agloval defies his father's expectations to conceal the truth from his kingdom and continue his lineage. Instead of Sh'eenaz using a potion to become human, Agloval drinks the potion himself to become a merman. He sacrifices his position on land, leaving the human world behind to live in the sea with Sh'eenaz and her people. Usveldt, disappointed, he blames the witcher for his loss of a son and legacy. But Geralt holds the king responsible, replying that it was his own ambition and ego that caused him to lose two sons, and that this was the legacy he deserved.


Following their success in aiding the town, they back at Essi's, and while they resting, she reflects on the situation. Now that Agloval and Sh'eenaz are happy, she acknowledge that their ability to resolve their own differences brings peace. Geralt admits to Essi that he could not have resolved the case without her help, it's not something he used to saying. In response to their closeness and the success of the mission, Essi urges Geralt to open his heart to people and let them into his life, and to stop holding himself back from emotional connection, though Geralt remains cynical about trusting others. And in that precise moment, they commits to their feelings, and both they share a moment of intimacy and a affair for the night. In the morning, Geralt is remorseful, but Essi tells him they don't need to speak, fully aware that they cannot give each other and the profound difference in their lives: she desires a family and stability, while Geralt is driven by his addicted to the open road and his yearning for Yennefer. They part amicably, without regrets. 

After witnessing Agloval and Sh'eenaz find happiness, Jaskier compose a melancholy ballad about the nature of sacrifice. Geralt and Jaskier depart from Bremervoort, while Geralt remarks how human rulers often damage their legacies because of pride. As for Essi, she is wonderful, but she doesn't understand Geralt's long-term perspective, like someone who's lived as long as he have, someone like Yennefer. He was about to mention her when Jaskier interrupted him. Though he laments his friend's romantic predicament, he assured Geralt that he would eventually find peace. The only certainty was that their journey was not over, and for their next adventure in the farthest corner of the Continent, Jaskier suggested they travel to Caingorn in the Dragon Mountains, far away to avoid any possible encounter with Yennefer. Geralt smiling briefly, they departed together, ready for their next adventure.[5]

### Hunting a Dragon[]


Geralt had just finished slaying a basilisk when he returned to find his hirers preparing to steal Roach and leave without paying, as Jaskier is trying to to stop them. They were approached by Borch Three Jackdaws and his two Zerrikanian companions, warriors Téa and Véa, killed one hirer's neck. Intimidated, the last hirer then turns over the promised payment to Geralt and flees in terror. Borch then introduces himself to Geralt and invites he and Jaskier along for a drink. They had sought Geralt out, hoping to gain his assistance in slaying a green dragon that had landed across the border in King Niedamir's mountains. Geralt listened as Borch told him that locals had spotted it and pursued it to try to take its treasure, but they had succeeded only in wounding the creature and angering it so much that it caused significant destruction in the area. The king, wanting the dragon dead before it could interfere with his imminent marriage to the princess of a rival kingdom, had commissioned a hunt to kill it, and four teams had signed on, Borch's being one of them. The winner would get the dragon's treasure hoard and the title of lord over one of King Niedamir's vassal states. 

Geralt initially declined Borch's offer to join his team as he didn't kill dragons. However, Borch persevered, as he needed one final adventure, and he thought that killing a dragon would bring him that. With a witcher on his team, he'd be unstoppable. Geralt remained unconvinced when he learned that joining them on the hunt were a group of dwarves and Reavers. However, his decision changes upon seeing Yennefer arrive at the tavern with the knight Eyck of Denesle in tow. He learned that she formed the fourth team. Her mere presence changed Geralt's mind, and he agreed to join Borch on his hunt, much to Jaskier's disapproval, as he was still afraid of Yennefer following the threats she'd made while demanding he use the djinn's last wish.

Geralt and Jaskier spoke to Yennefer for the first time in years. She expressed her annoyance and couldn't help but wonder why she kept running into Geralt, despite having walked the earth for decades and never meeting a single witcher. She explained that she was there to accompany Sir Eyck as he was to slay the dragon. Geralt even hold back his jealousy at Yennefer's closeness to her escort. 

While on the path to kill the dragon, Geralt and Borch were only a few feet behind Yennefer and Eyck. In that time, Borch realized that Geralt was in love with her. They reached the hillside scorched by the dragon, a creature that tended to avoid people. Geralt questioned why it hadn't yet left. Borch replied that the beast must be becoming desperate. Jaskier suddenly came face-to-face with a hirikka while picking berries for Tèa and Vèa. Geralt surmised that the creature was starving and of no danger to them. Eyck completely disregarded him and killed it.

All four groups decided to settle down on the mountainside. Geralt, Jaskier, Borch, Tèa, Vèa, Yennefer, Eyck, Yarpen Zigrin , the leader of the dwarves, and Boholt, the leader of the Reavers, roasted the hirikka and feasted. However, Borch warned Eyck against eating a certain part of the creature, a warning Eyck ignored. Boholt interrupted them and made a lewd remark towards Yennefer. Eyck took his leave as his stomach started to gurgle after failing to heed Borch's warning. They proceeded to discuss how the rightful son of Nilfgaard had returned and started burning through the south, with the mage Fringilla Vigo aiding him. It wouldn't be long before they tried to take Sodden, then Temeria, Redania, and Cintra, but Jaskier claimed that Queen Calanthe would die before letting them take what's hers.

Jaskier doubted the mere existence of dragons until Geralt assured him that they were real, though their numbers were dwindling. Green dragons were the most common, red dragons were less so, and black dragons were the rarest. Borch corrected him and stated that golden dragons were, in fact, the rarest. Geralt retorted that they were a myth. Whether that was true or not, gold dragons met the same fate as any other dragon: they'd died out.


Yennefer awakened the following morning to find Eyck missing. Yarpen found him dead by a tree with his pants down and throat slit. Nevertheless, the hunt continued. Yarpen suspected that the Reavers had killed Eyck, and so he knew of a shortcut across the mountains that he only shared with Geralt, Jaskier, Borch, Tèa, and Vèa, proposing a truce until they reached the next peak. Geralt tried to convince Yennefer to join them on the shorter path. Much like Yarpen, Yennefer suspected that Boholt had killed her escort before he could accomplish the one task she needed him for. Geralt asked Yennefer what she's really doing on this hunt. Yennefer revealed that dragons are said to possess certain healing properties. Geralt openly mocks her idea and informed her that fertility cures using fresh dragon hearts were a myth. Geralt also didn't believe she'd make a good mother, and asks what she could possibly want with a child. Yennefer explained that she wanted her choice to bear a child back. Geralt informed her that witchers can't bear children either. They were made sterile because their lifestyle wasn't suited for children. Unfortunately his argument was muted somewhat, when Geralt then unintentionally revealed to Yennefer his Child Surprise. She points out to him on lecturing her on having a child when he has cheated destiny to steal one. Geralt tries to change the subject by telling her of the dwarves' shortcut. Yennefer insists she can take care of herself, but Geralt counsels that doesn't mean she has to always refuse others' help. 

Yarpen and his men guided Geralt, Jaskier, Yennefer, Borch, Tèa, and Vèa to a fairly narrow path lined with wooden boards alongside the mountain, a tight squeeze for anyone larger than a dwarf. A board broke beneath Borch's feet, and he fell, as did Tèa and Vèa. The only thing preventing them from plummeting to the ground was Geralt holding on to the other end of the chain. Borch told Geralt to let him go. When Geralt refused, Borch let go of the chain, shortly followed by Tèa and Vèa, and the three of them disappeared within the fog as they fell to the ground below. 

Jaskier told Geralt that he'd done his best to save them. There wasn't much he could do. He suggested that they give up on the hunt and, provided Geralt gives him another chance to prove himself as a worthy travel companion, they head for the coast.

Geralt entered Yennefer's tent, which she had placed a spell on to make much larger on the inside than outside. Yennefer admitted to being worried for Geralt on the mountain. He found her scent mesmerizing. He confessed that the moment he dreaded most every time she left was when it faded. Yennefer reminded Geralt that he had left first in Rinde. She had woken up in the destroyed house, and he was gone. Geralt asked for forgiveness, and the two kissed and made love. 

After, both in bed, Yennefer questioned if the rumors were true about witchers being devoid of human emotion. Geralt explained that it was false: people said whatever justified despising his kind. If the choice had been up to him, Yennefer wondered what Geralt would've been instead of a witcher. Much like Geralt, Yennefer didn't have much of a choice in being a mage. She always dreamed of becoming important to someone someday. As he began to fall asleep, Geralt assured Yennefer that she was important to him now.

Yennefer woke up the following morning to find Geralt still at her side. At a quick pace, they could make it back to the Pensive Dragon before sundown; however, Yennefer had no intentions of turning around. She was still intent on killing the dragon. She then rushed off to the dragon's cave after noticing the dwarves were already ahead of her.

Geralt eventually caught up to Yennefer in the dragon's cave, only to find out that Tèa and Vèa were alive, and the green dragon was dead. But she was not alone. Enter a gold dragon, which revealed itself to be Borch. When the dragoness was injured, her cry was heard by Villentretenmerth, but the egg could not be moved, or the life inside it would die, which is why she had attacked instead of fleeing. She was protecting her baby by scaring the people away from her and her egg. That's when Borch, Tèa, and Vèa had heard about the king's hunt and realized they needed to keep their enemies close. So, Borch had come to find Geralt, the knight who was taught to save dragons rather than kill them. As Borch finished explaining this, Boholt and his gang of Reavers arrived, forcing Geralt, Yennefer, Tèa, and Vèa to defend the dragon and the egg.

Geralt and Yennefer defended one entrance to the cave while Tèa and Vèa defended the other. During the fight against the Reavers, Yennefer kissed Geralt to give him the energy to use his Aard sign to blast their attackers away from the cave entrance. They were faced with Boholt and one remaining Reaver. Yennefer made sure that it was she who killed Boholt. Afterwards, Borch paid off Yarpen and his men, offering them teeth belonging to the green dragon to take to the king as proof of its demise so that they could claim the king's reward.

Borch thanked Geralt and Yennefer for all their help in defending him and his family. He noted that he sees why Geralt didn't want to lose Yennefer. Yennefer questioned the meaning behind this, and Geralt revealed that he was referring to Rinde and their encounter with the djinn. That was why they couldn't escape each other: Geralt had wished for it. Yennefer took that to mean that her feelings for Geralt were magic, though he insisted that wasn't true. An argument ensued, leading the two to part ways. Borch saved them both a lot of hurt with a little pain now. He revealed that Yennefer would never regain her womb, and Geralt would lose Yennefer. Borch informed Geralt that he was still missing his legacy and destiny.

Geralt grew angry and lashed out at Jaskier, blaming him for all his recent troubles—the Child Surprise, the djinn, all of it could be traced back to him. Geralt exclaimed that if life could give him one blessing, it would be to take Jaskier off his hands. With that being said, Jaskier got the story from the others to write his song and departed.[6]

### Imprisoned in Cintra[]


Later, Geralt returned to Cintra, where he arranged a meeting with Mousesack to ensure his Child of Surprise was healthy and being cared for. Mousesack corrected Geralt that "he" was a girl, and informed him that Princess Cirilla had been raised by Calanthe since her parents had died at sea. Geralt warned Mousesack that he had seen an army of Nilfgaardian soldiers making camp at the Amelia Pass, threateningly close to Cintra. Mousesack assured Geralt that the queen had done everything she could to ensure her family's safety in the twelve years he had been gone from Cintra. Geralt suddenly spotted men moving through the tunnels. He suspected that Calanthe had learned of his arrival and sent assassins to kill him, to prevent him from claiming Ciri as his Child of Surprise and leaving with her. Surrounded and outnumbered, Geralt held Mousesack hostage. To reach him, they would first have had to kill Mousesack. They charged with their weapons, and so Mousesack was forced to portal himself and Geralt to safety. 

Geralt and Mousesack confronted Calanthe. Geralt had stayed away for twelve years since he'd left Cintra before Ciri's birth and had planned on staying that way until Calanthe had sent eight men to kill him. Geralt had come to protect Ciri, and when Calanthe tried to buy Geralt off, Mousesack interjected that money can't undo the Law of Surprise. Kings who've tried to outbid destiny ended up on pikes. Danek and Lazlo drew their swords as Geralt approached. He advised Calanthe to give Ciri over to him if she had any doubt that Ciri wasn't safe in Cintra amid the looming threat of Nilfgaard's invasion. Geralt promised to take her somewhere safe, protect her, and bring her back to Calanthe unharmed when the threat was resolved. Calanthe reluctantly agreed to let Ciri leave with him and exclaimed to the townspeople that the Law of Surprise had been called.

Geralt entered Calanthe's chambers to meet Ciri. Unbeknownst to him, Calanthe had no intention of giving her up and had instead disguised someone else's child as Ciri, handing her over to Geralt. Mousesack watched on silently. Calanthe then told Geralt that she'd summon him when Ciri was ready to leave. Geralt exited Calanthe's chambers and followed the passageway through a hidden door that magically opened. The tunnel led him outside the castle, where the girl impersonating Ciri was saying goodbye to her friends, the real Ciri being amongst them.

Geralt confronted Calanthe after realizing that she'd tried to send him off with an imposter that wasn't Princess Cirilla and for trying to defy fate. Calanthe insisted that Ciri was safe with her until the day came that she would take over the throne, refusing to let her go with him. Furthermore, she refused to give Geralt's words any further thought. The last time she'd listened to him, she'd let a hedgehog into her court, which ultimately resulted in Pavetta's death. Calanthe even criticized Geralt's capacity to raise Ciri, citing his own abandonment by his mother, and she refused to lose Ciri the same way she'd lost her daughter. She ordered Eist, who has just returned from Skellige and now as King of Cintra, to get Geralt out of her kingdom.

Geralt recalled when Eist honored the Law of Surprise. Eist explained that it was before he'd had a granddaughter. Assuming Nilfgaard attacked Cintra, Eist would be right by Calanthe's side. Geralt accused him of putting too much faith in the Queen, but he wasn't there when Pavetta had died. Calanthe would wake up howling in the night, the Lioness, nearly broken. Someone who was able to pull themselves out of that would have Eist's confidence until his final day. He asked Geralt to promise not to come back. When Geralt refused, Eist had him imprisoned.

Geralt plotted his escape while trapped in the dungeon of Queen Calanthe's castle as Nilfgaard invaded. He attacked one of the guards and freed himself from his cell. Geralt made it outside, where he disposed of several Nilfgaard invaders. Geralt watched from the shadows as the Nilfgaard army took Cintra. Suddenly, he heard a loud thud. Upon investigation, he discovered it was the queen. She'd jumped out of her window and committed suicide. Geralt ran back into the castle to find Ciri. Instead, he found several Nilfgaardian soldiers, all of whom he murdered when they refused to tell him where to find her.[7]

### Bitten by a Ghoul[]

Cintra went up in flames in the aftermath of the Nilfgaardian attack. Geralt remained in the castle, still in search of Princess Cirilla. He left the kingdom after realizing that she was already gone, his previous promise to Calanthe to protect her granddaughter ringing hollowly in his ears.

During his travels, he came across a decimated Cintran refugee camp. There, he crossed paths with a merchant named Yurga, giving the bodies a proper burial, although Geralt initially assumed he was a grave robber. Geralt sensed danger and advised the man to leave the grounds. Instead, Yurga stayed to ensure the bodies were properly laid to rest, but Geralt refused his request to help, turning to leave for Kaer Morhen instead. Moments later, however, Yurga was attacked by ghouls, who emerged from the ground beneath his feet. Luckily, Geralt returned to save Yurga, who cautioned Geralt against the fatality of a single ghoul bite. Geralt sent Yurga away to safety, but he was bitten while slaying the creatures. The bite took effect almost instantly, and Geralt passed out, making one last comment to Roach about how this was a fitting end for him.

Yurga travelled through the woods of Sodden with Geralt going in and out of consciousness in the back of his carriage. The ghoul bite had made him delirious, but he was still alive due to his heightened witcher fortitude. In his delirious state, Geralt recalled moments from his childhood with his mother, Visenna, when she had instilled in him a moral code: to "live and let live" whenever possible.

Geralt awakened more fully in the back of Yurga's carriage. He inquired about the nearby explosions he could hear, and Yurga informed him that Nilfgaard was attacking Sodden. Geralt then drank a black elixir from his bag and poured some on his wound. He requested that Yurga take him to the Blue Mountains, where someone could save him. In his delusional state, he recalled more memories with his mother, including one where he had been in the back of a carriage that she steered. Eventually, she had stopped and asked him to get water from a nearby creek. By the time he returned, his mother was gone, but Vesemir was waiting for him.


Still infected by his ghoulish bite, Geralt's condition worsened. He began hallucinating Renfri and Yennefer treating his wound. Lastly, he hallucinated actually seeing his mother in front of him. She explained that he had been saved by his pulse, which was four times slower than a normal man's. She heard a merchant's cry for help and decided to help, as healing was her profession. She said to him, "People linked by destiny will always find each other." Geralt grew so angry at the sight of her.
